messages.message: No MC support (instant, from measured curve)

message.p: How the response that answers off-axis, near-field and other-distance queries is built. All three use this detector's measured efficiency where it has one - what differs is how much Monte Carlo backs the distance and angle dependence.

ul.li: Full MC characterization - Monte Carlo over the full energy×angle(×distance) grid of the selected profile, then corrected to the measured efficiency (see "Measured eff." below). Most accurate, especially near the detector and off-axis; most run time.

Quick MC (transfer) - Monte Carlo only along the on-axis energy backbone (plus, optionally, a few source-angle anchors); the exact ray-traced geometry then carries the response to other distances and angles (EFFTRAN-style efficiency transfer). Corrected to the measured efficiency the same way Full MC is. Roughly a tenth of the Monte Carlo - typically around a minute. On-axis accuracy is about 1% beyond a few detector-widths; queries near contact or far off-axis are flagged and carry an honestly inflated uncertainty.

No MC support - no Monte Carlo at all: the measured efficiency points (or the fitted curve) are anchored at their measurement distance and transferred to other distances/angles through the ray-traced geometry - so here the measured efficiency IS the anchor, rather than a correction applied to a computed response. Instant and deterministic, and it rebuilds automatically as you edit the geometry. The classic lab efficiency-transfer workflow, made 3-D and Rayleigh-aware. Needs a measured efficiency to work from.

message.p: With no method at all, a detector answers every distance with its on-axis efficiency scaled by solid angle, and cannot answer off-axis at all.

messages.message: Currently a quick transfer response; a Full MC characterization is more accurate near-field and off-axis.

message.p: Controls how close to the detector the response stays accurate - i.e. how much extra Monte Carlo is spent characterizing the near-field. All three profiles cover the full front hemisphere (source angle 0° on-axis through 90° grazing) and the detector's whole energy range; they differ only in the closest distance they model. (Sources behind the detector face - angles > 90°, e.g. Marinelli beakers - are not modeled by any profile.)

ul.li: Far-field only - no near-field model at all. Accurate from roughly a few detector-widths outward; queries closer than that are flagged (not silently corrected). Cheapest. Use for fixed, large-standoff installations or search detectors.
General (default) - adds a near-field model down to about one detector transverse size (a few cm). Covers typical lab bench and hand-held measurements. Moderate extra cost.

Extra near detail - scans the near-field denser and all the way down to contact (about half a detector size, ~0.5 cm), with fine angular coverage close-in. Use for contact, well, or swipe counting, or anything held right against the endcap. Most Monte Carlo, but the only profile accurate at contact off-axis.

message.p: The per-node Monte-Carlo statistical target: how tightly each point of the response is computed. Tighter means less statistical noise baked into the stored response, at more run time (cost scales roughly as 1 / precision² - halving the target is about 4× the work).

ul.li: Fast (1%) - a quick preview, or small/high-efficiency detectors.
Normal (0.3%) - a good balance for most detectors (default).
Balanced (relaxed high-E) - keeps low-energy points tight but relaxes the expensive high-energy points, for about a 2× faster run at nearly the same accuracy.
Thorough (0.1%) - a high-quality reference; noticeably slower.
Custom - enter your own per-node target (e.g. 0.2%).

message.p: This is the statistical precision only; the response's overall accuracy also depends on how finely the energy/angle/distance grids are placed, so tightening precision helps but has diminishing returns.

messages.message: Correct to this detector's measured efficiency

message.p: A Monte-Carlo response says what a detector of this shape would do; the measured efficiency says what this detector actually does. When checked, the generated response is corrected by an energy-dependent factor (and its covariance) so it reproduces the measured efficiency, while the Monte Carlo keeps supplying the distance and angle dependence.
Un-check to get the raw computed response, uncorrected - useful for judging how well the geometry alone reproduces the measurement.

message.p: How many source angles the quick Monte Carlo anchors the transfer at.

ul.li: On-axis only - the geometry kernel alone carries the angular dependence. Off-axis full-energy-peak efficiencies are good to roughly 3-4%, and for HPGe the total efficiency (used by cascade-summing corrections) can drift off-axis. Fine for on-axis measurements.
3 angles - a few extra MC anchors versus on-axis only; brings off-axis full-energy-peak accuracy under about 1% and tabulates a real angular total-efficiency shape (recommended, especially for HPGe).

message.p: The source-to-detector distance the efficiency curve is valid at - the anchor the transfer holds fixed. Pre-filled from where the curve is pinned to data: its stated measurement distance when it has one, otherwise a comfortably far-field distance. When the DRF carries raw measured points at a single distance, the points pin it and it cannot be edited.
Distances are measured from the detector face (the front of the endcap).

message.p: Source-to-detector distance for the absolute efficiency curves (per emitted gamma). Each curve is the full-energy-peak efficiency versus energy at a source angle of 0°, 22.5°, 45° and the largest angle the response models (near grazing) from the detector axis. In the intrinsic view the dashed line is the angle-flat far-field (infinite-plane) reference. The shaded band around each curve is its 1-sigma uncertainty, and a curve whose legend is annotated (e.g. "near-field unmodeled") is outside the response's validated regime at this distance. Intrinsic efficiency (per gamma striking the face) is distance-independent in the far field.
